tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Day 3, 0800: 83-year-old client admitted 2 days ago from home with aspiration pneumonia. History of Parkinson disease and moderate dementia; wears bilateral hearing aids. Oriented to self only. Moans and grimaces with turning but cannot state where discomfort is. Bedfast; makes occasional slight changes in position without help. Slides down in bed when the head of the bed is raised for meals; requires 2-person assist to reposition. Incontinent of urine and stool; linen changed 3 times overnight. Eats about 25% of pureed meals and refuses the oral supplement. Spouse visits daily and states the client ‘barely moved from the recliner’ for the week before admission.

Skin: Sacrum — 4 × 3 cm area of nonblanchable redness, skin intact, warmer than surrounding skin. Right heel — 2 × 2 cm area of nonblanchable redness, skin intact, spongy (boggy) on palpation. Left heel — 1 × 1 cm intact blister filled with clear serous fluid. Left ischial tuberosity — 1.5 × 1 cm shallow open area with a pink, moist wound bed; no slough. Radial and pedal pulses 2+ bilaterally.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours
  • Dysphagia (pureed) diet; HOB ≥ 30° during meals and for 1 hour after
  • Oxygen 2 L/min via nasal cannula; titrate to SpO₂ ≥ 92%
  • Pressure-injury prevention protocol; reposition per protocol
  • Wound care nurse and dietitian consults
  • Weigh daily

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Braden Scale. The nurse reviews an excerpt from the 0800 note. Click to highlight the findings that place the client at increased risk for developing additional pressure injuries.
questions.passage: The 83-year-old client wears {{bilateral hearing aids}} and is {{oriented to self only}}. The client {{slides down in bed when the head of the bed is raised}} and is {{incontinent of urine and stool}}. The client {{eats about 25% of pureed meals}} and has a temperature of {{38.1 °C (100.6 °F)}}. {{Radial and pedal pulses are 2+ bilaterally}}, and the {{spouse visits daily and wants to help with care}}.
optionRationales: Not a risk factor. Hearing loss corrected with aids does not reduce the client’s ability to sense or respond to pressure.
Risk factor. Decreased mental status reduces the ability to perceive and respond to pressure-related discomfort (Braden sensory perception 2).
Risk factor. Sliding down in bed creates shear and friction, which distort and tear deep blood vessels (friction & shear 1).
Risk factor. Urine and stool add moisture, enzymes, and urea that macerate the skin and lower its tolerance to pressure (moisture 2).
Risk factor. Eating 25% of meals means inadequate protein and calories for tissue maintenance (nutrition 1); serum albumin is also low.
Risk factor. Excess body heat raises metabolic rate and oxygen demand, worsening ischemia in tissue that is under pressure.
Not a risk factor. Palpable 2+ pulses indicate adequate peripheral arterial flow.
Not a risk factor. An involved spouse is a strength who can be taught prevention measures.
questions.rationale: Pressure-injury risk factors include decreased mental status or sensation, immobility, shear and friction, moisture from incontinence, poor nutrition, and excess body heat. This client’s Braden total of 9 reflects very high risk, and every highlighted finding maps to a low subscale or a slide-listed risk factor. Normal pulses and a supportive spouse are not risk factors.
questions.takeaway: Map each cue to a Braden subscale (or to fever/heat) to find the client’s risk factors.
questions.hintContent: The Braden scale scores sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear. Excess body heat is another listed risk factor.
questions.hintStrategy: Go through the passage one finding at a time and ask: ‘Does this lower tissue tolerance or raise pressure, shear, or moisture?’ Highlight only findings that do.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes. For each skin finding, indicate the stage of pressure injury the nurse should document.
rows: Sacrum: 4 × 3 cm nonblanchable redness, skin intact, warmer than surrounding skin
Right heel: 2 × 2 cm nonblanchable redness, skin intact, spongy (boggy) on palpation
Left heel: 1 × 1 cm intact blister filled with clear serous fluid
Left ischial tuberosity: 1.5 × 1 cm shallow open area with a pink, moist wound bed and no slough
optionRationales: Stage 1: intact skin with nonblanchable redness; warmth reflects inflammation. There is no open skin.
Stage 1: intact skin with nonblanchable redness; spongy, boggy tissue (edema) is another cue of damage beneath the skin.
Stage 2: a blister reflects partial-thickness loss of the epidermis and possibly the dermis.
Stage 2: a shallow, open, pink, moist wound is partial-thickness loss; no subcutaneous tissue is visible.
questions.rationale: Stage 1 is nonblanchable redness of intact skin. Stage 2 is partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and possibly the dermis, appearing as a clear blister or a shallow, open, pink wound. Stage 3 would require full-thickness loss into subcutaneous tissue, which is not present.
questions.takeaway: Intact nonblanchable = Stage 1; clear blister or shallow pink open area = Stage 2.
questions.hintContent: For each finding, decide whether the skin is intact, partially lost, or lost through its full thickness.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each row independently. Look first at whether the skin is intact, then at how deep any open area is.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Braden Scale. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The client's Braden total of {0} indicates {1} risk. The open area on the left ischial tuberosity is a {2} pressure injury, so the nurse adds the nursing diagnosis {3}.

options: mild
moderate
very high
Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Risk for infection
Potential for impaired skin integrity
Situational low self-esteem

questions.rationale: The subscores total 9 (2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1); a Braden score of 9 or less indicates very high risk. The ischial wound is a shallow, open, pink area — partial-thickness loss, or Stage 2. Once the skin is open, the client is at risk for infection. "Potential for impaired skin integrity" no longer fits because the skin is already impaired, and nothing in the notes suggests low self-esteem.
questions.takeaway: Low Braden = high risk; an open wound adds Risk for infection.
questions.hintContent: Add the six subscores. Then recall which nursing diagnoses apply once the skin is open.
questions.hintStrategy: Answer the blanks in order; the first two depend on arithmetic and the Braden cut-offs, and the last must fit the wound you staged.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Braden Scale, and Orders. Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Float both heels with pillows placed lengthwise under the calves
Request a specialty support surface such as a low-air-loss mattress
Massage the reddened sacral area during each turn to restore circulation
Cleanse with a mild cleanser and apply a barrier cream after each incontinent episode
Turn the client to a 90° side-lying position to keep pressure off the sacrum
Place a ring cushion under the sacrum when the client sits up in the chair
Collaborate with the dietitian to increase protein and calorie intake
optionRationales: Correct. Floating the heels removes pressure from the right heel Stage 1 injury and the left heel blister.
Correct. A client at very high risk with existing injuries needs a pressure-redistribution surface such as a low-air-loss bed.
Incorrect. Massage over reddened bony prominences damages fragile capillaries and deeper tissue.
Correct. Prompt, gentle cleansing and a barrier product protect the skin from urine and stool.
Incorrect. A 90° side-lying position places full pressure on the greater trochanter; a 30° tilt with pillows is preferred.
Incorrect. Ring (doughnut) devices reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue.
Correct. Nutrition subscale 1, low albumin, and open skin call for increased protein and calories.
questions.rationale: Plan care around each low Braden subscale: pressure redistribution (support surface, 30° tilt, heel floating), moisture management (gentle cleansing and barrier products), and nutrition (dietitian collaboration, supplements). Massage, 90° side-lying, and donut devices increase tissue damage.
questions.takeaway: Target every low Braden subscale — offload, keep dry, feed, and avoid massage and donuts.
questions.hintContent: Recall which practices increase pressure or damage capillaries and which redistribute pressure or protect the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own as true or false for this client. Link each correct option to a specific low subscale or skin finding in the exhibit.

Day 3, 1000: UAP reports the client ‘slid all the way down to the footboard.’ Head of bed found at 45°; breakfast finished at 0800. Client’s heels are resting on the mattress. Sheets wrinkled and damp beneath the client. Client grimacing.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours
  • Dysphagia (pureed) diet; HOB ≥ 30° during meals and for 1 hour after
  • Oxygen 2 L/min via nasal cannula; titrate to SpO₂ ≥ 92%
  • Pressure-injury prevention protocol; reposition per protocol
  • Wound care nurse and dietitian consults
  • Weigh daily

questions.stem: Refer to the 1000 entry in the Nurses' Notes and the Orders. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply a transparent film dressing over the sacral Stage 1 area to reduce friction
Lower the HOB to 30° or less and lift the client up in bed with two staff
Raise the head of the bed to high-Fowler position to prevent aspiration of oral secretions
Ask the UAP to pull the client up by the arms after the next meal is finished
optionRationales: Incorrect. A film dressing may reduce friction, but it does not stop the ongoing shear and pressure causing the problem right now.
Correct. Breakfast ended 2 hours ago, so the HOB no longer needs to be elevated. Lowering the HOB to ≤ 30° and lifting (not dragging) the client removes the shear force immediately.
Incorrect. High-Fowler position increases shear and sacral pressure; the order requires HOB ≥ 30° only during meals and for 1 hour after.
Incorrect. Pulling by the arms risks shoulder injury and drags the skin (friction and shear), and delaying repositioning prolongs tissue injury.
questions.rationale: The client has slid down with the HOB at 45° two hours after eating — sustained shear and pressure on the sacrum. The first action is to lower the HOB to 30° or less (the aspiration-precaution window has ended) and reposition the client using a lift sheet and two caregivers. The nurse then floats the heels, changes the damp linen, and addresses pain.
questions.takeaway: Stop shear first: lower the HOB to ≤ 30° when safe and lift — never drag — the client.
questions.hintContent: Shear occurs when the skeleton slides down while the skin stays fixed to the sheet; it is worst with HOB elevation above 30°.
questions.hintStrategy: ‘First’ means the action that removes the active cause of injury. Check the order’s time limit for HOB elevation against the time of the last meal.

Skin reassessment: See findings in the question.

questions.stem: Refer to the Day 7 Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Braden Scale. The nurse reassesses the client on Day 7. For each finding, indicate whether it shows that the plan of care has been effective or ineffective.
rows: Sacral redness now blanches and fades within 30 minutes of turning
Left heel blister has been reabsorbed; skin intact and pink, heel floated off the mattress
Left ischial wound now 0.4 cm deep with visible yellow fat
Eats 75% of meals and drinks two protein supplements daily
New 2 × 2 cm area of nonblanchable redness over the left greater trochanter
optionRationales: Effective. Redness that blanches and fades after pressure is removed indicates restored capillary flow — the Stage 1 injury has resolved.
Effective. The Stage 2 blister is healing while the heel is offloaded.
Ineffective. Visible fat means full-thickness loss; the wound has progressed from Stage 2 to Stage 3 and the plan needs revision.
Effective. Improved intake (Braden nutrition 1 → 3) supports tissue repair.
Ineffective. A new Stage 1 injury over the trochanter suggests positioning is placing weight on the hip (for example, side-lying beyond a 30° tilt).
questions.rationale: Evaluation compares current findings with expected outcomes. Resolved sacral redness, a healing heel blister, and improved nutrition show progress. Deterioration of the ischial wound to full thickness and a new trochanteric injury show the plan is not meeting goals, so the nurse reassesses positioning, the support surface, and turning technique and modifies the plan.
questions.takeaway: New or deeper injuries = revise the plan; resolving redness and better intake = keep going.
questions.hintContent: Recall what blanchable versus nonblanchable redness means, and which tissue becomes visible when a wound becomes full thickness.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, ask: ‘Is this better, the same, or worse than on Day 3?’ Stable offloaded injuries can count as effective.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1400: 58-year-old client with T10 paraplegia and type 2 diabetes admitted from home with a known Stage 3 right ischial pressure injury. Wound 5 × 4 × 1.5 cm; moderate thick green drainage with a foul odor after cleansing. Periwound skin red, warm, and indurated, with redness extending 3 cm from the wound edge (outlined with a skin marker). Client reports increased pain at the wound and feeling ‘achy and hot.’ Uses a foam wheelchair cushion that is 6 years old.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Wound culture now
  • IV antibiotic as prescribed — start after the culture is obtained
  • Bed rest on low-air-loss mattress; no sitting
  • Wound care nurse and dietitian consults

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, Laboratory Results, and Orders. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Normal inflammatory phase of healing
Wound infection of the pressure injury
Moisture-related skin breakdown
Allergic reaction to the dressing adhesive
Obtain the wound culture as prescribed before the first antibiotic dose
Place a ring cushion under the ischium so the client can sit up for meals
Massage the indurated skin around the wound to improve blood flow
Administer the prescribed IV antibiotic after the culture is obtained
Increase sitting time in the wheelchair to prevent pneumonia
Braden sensory perception score
Temperature
Serum potassium
Blanch response of the heels
Extent of periwound erythema

condition: Incorrect. Normal inflammation causes mild redness close to the wound edge early in healing — not purulent, foul drainage, fever, and a high WBC in an established wound.
Correct. Increased pain, purulent green drainage, odor, spreading warm redness, fever, and an elevated WBC are signs of wound infection.
Incorrect. Moisture damage is superficial and diffuse and does not cause fever or purulent drainage.
Incorrect. An allergic reaction would cause itching and redness under the adhesive, not purulent drainage and fever.
actions: Correct. A culture identifies the organism; it is collected before antibiotics start so the results are accurate.
Incorrect. Ring cushions reduce blood flow, and sitting puts pressure directly on the ischial wound; the order is bed rest.
Incorrect. Massaging inflamed tissue causes further damage.
Correct. Give the prescribed IV antibiotic promptly once the culture is collected.
Incorrect. Sitting increases pressure on the ischial wound; the order is bed rest with no sitting.
parameters: Incorrect. Braden subscales assess risk, not response to treatment of infection.
Correct. Resolution of fever indicates response to antibiotic therapy.
Incorrect. Potassium is not affected by this infection or its treatment in any expected way.
Incorrect. Heel blanch response monitors prevention, not the ischial infection.
Correct. Redness that stays inside or recedes from the marked border shows the infection is responding; spread beyond the border indicates failure.

questions.rationale: The cue cluster (increased pain, purulent foul drainage, spreading warm redness, fever, WBC 15,800/mm³) indicates an infected pressure injury. The slides direct the nurse to recognize infection early and report changes to the provider. Collect the culture before the first antibiotic dose, then give the antibiotic as ordered. Temperature and the marked border of redness are the most direct measures of response. Sitting on the wound, ring cushions, and massage would worsen the condition.
questions.takeaway: Infected pressure injury: culture first, then antibiotics; trend fever and the redness border.
questions.hintContent: Recall the local and systemic signs of wound infection and why cultures must precede antibiotics.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the condition first; then choose only actions and parameters that directly treat or measure that condition.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1000: 81-year-old client, day 2 after surgical repair of a hip fracture. Confused at night; on bed rest. Incontinent of urine; linens found damp. Eating about 30% of meals. Night-shift report states the client has been lying on the back since 0600 because the client "fights turning." Sacrum: 3 × 3 cm area of redness, skin intact; redness does not blanch and has not faded 30 minutes after the client was turned to the side; warmer than surrounding skin. Heels pink and blanchable. Braden score 11.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Normal blanchable redness from pressure
Stage 1 pressure injury of the sacrum
Stage 2 pressure injury of the sacrum
Wound infection of the sacrum
Reposition off the sacrum at least every 2 hours using a draw sheet
Massage the sacral area to restore blood flow
Cleanse with a mild cleanser, pat dry, and apply a barrier cream after each incontinent episode
Place a doughnut cushion under the sacrum
Raise the head of the bed to 60° for comfort
Sacral skin color and blanch response at each turn
Serum potassium level
Braden scale moisture and mobility subscores
Pupil size and reactivity
Bowel sounds

condition: Incorrect. Normal redness blanches and fades after pressure is removed; this area does not.
Correct. Nonblanchable redness of intact skin over a bony prominence, with warmth, is a Stage 1 pressure injury.
Incorrect. Stage 2 involves a blister or shallow open area; the skin is intact.
Incorrect. There is no open wound, drainage, odor, or fever.
actions: Correct. Pressure relief is the priority; reposition at least every 2 hours and lift with a draw sheet to avoid shear.
Incorrect. Massage over reddened bony prominences damages tissue further.
Correct. Managing moisture from incontinence protects the skin from maceration.
Incorrect. Doughnut devices reduce blood flow to surrounding tissue.
Incorrect. HOB above 30° increases shear on the sacrum.
parameters: Correct. Return of blanching and fading redness show the injury is resolving; open skin would show progression.
Incorrect. Potassium does not reflect pressure injury status.
Correct. Improving moisture and mobility subscores show that the main risk factors are being controlled.
Incorrect. Pupil response is a neurologic assessment unrelated to this problem.
Incorrect. Bowel sounds do not track the pressure injury.

questions.rationale: Nonblanchable redness of intact skin over the sacrum after hours of unrelieved pressure is a Stage 1 pressure injury. Care targets the causes: reposition at least every 2 hours with proper lifting, keep the skin clean and dry with a barrier product, and avoid massage, doughnut devices, and HOB elevation above 30°. The nurse monitors the area's color and blanch response and reassesses Braden subscores.
questions.takeaway: Stage 1: get off it, keep it dry, and recheck the blanch response.
questions.hintContent: Recall how the blanch test separates normal redness from a Stage 1 injury, and the prevention measures on the implementation slide.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the condition first; then choose only actions that relieve pressure or moisture and parameters that show whether the skin is recovering.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Assessment (Dark Skin)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 58-year-old client with darkly pigmented skin who has been on bed rest for 4 days after a stroke. The nurse reviews the skin assessment documented by a student nurse. Click to highlight the findings that suggest a pressure injury is developing.
questions.passage: Skin assessed in natural light. Left greater trochanter: {{4 × 3 cm area that is darker and more purplish than the surrounding skin}}, {{warmer to the touch than adjacent skin}}, and {{firm and indurated on palpation}}; client {{reports tenderness when the area is touched}}. {{Dry, flaky skin on both shins}}. {{Capillary refill in the fingers is 2 seconds}}. {{Sacral skin is uniform in color with the surrounding skin}}. {{Oral mucous membranes are moist}}.
optionRationales: Suggests injury. In dark skin, erythema may not be visible; a localized darker, purple, or bluish area over a bony prominence is a key sign.
Suggests injury. Localized warmth reflects inflammation beneath the skin.
Suggests injury. Induration or firmness (or bogginess) signals tissue damage under intact skin.
Suggests injury. Localized pain or tenderness over a pressure point often precedes visible change.
Not specific. Dry, flaky shins reflect xerosis and need moisturizing, but not a pressure injury.
Normal. Capillary refill of 2 seconds is normal peripheral perfusion.
Normal. Uniform sacral color suggests no injury at that site.
Normal. Moist mucous membranes indicate adequate hydration.
questions.rationale: Blanching and redness are hard to see in darkly pigmented skin, so the nurse relies on color change compared with surrounding skin (darker, purple, bluish), temperature change (warmth or coolness), tissue consistency (induration, bogginess, edema), and pain. Good natural or halogen light improves visual assessment.
questions.takeaway: Dark skin: compare color, temperature, texture, and pain — don’t wait for redness.
questions.hintContent: Recall which senses besides sight the nurse uses to detect early pressure injury when erythema is hard to see.
questions.hintStrategy: Group each finding as abnormal-and-localized to a bony prominence versus normal or unrelated. Only the first group suggests pressure injury.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Implementation (Teaching)
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a 76-year-old client with right hemiplegia after a stroke who is cared for by an adult daughter. The nurse documents the daughter's description of her care routine. Click to highlight the practices that indicate a need for further teaching.
questions.passage: Daughter states she {{turns her mother at least every 2 hours during the day}} and {{rubs lotion firmly into the red areas over the tailbone}}. She {{keeps the head of the bed at 60° most of the day so her mother can watch TV}} and {{uses a rubber ring cushion when her mother sits in the recliner}}. She {{places a pillow lengthwise under the calves so the heels float}}, {{washes the skin with warm water and a mild cleanser}}, {{sprinkles cornstarch in the groin after incontinence}}, and {{offers a protein shake between meals}}.
optionRationales: Appropriate. Repositioning at least every 2 hours is the standard for bedbound clients.
Needs teaching. Massaging reddened bony prominences damages capillaries and deep tissue.
Needs teaching. HOB above 30° for long periods increases sacral pressure and shear.
Needs teaching. Ring (donut) cushions compress the surrounding tissue and reduce blood flow.
Appropriate. Floating the heels removes pressure from the heels.
Appropriate. Warm (not hot) water and mild cleansers protect the skin barrier.
Needs teaching. Powders and cornstarch cake with moisture and irritate the skin; a barrier cream or film is used instead.
Appropriate. Extra protein and calories between meals support skin integrity.
questions.rationale: Prevention teaching includes repositioning, heel floating, gentle cleansing, nutrition, and avoiding harmful practices: massage over bony prominences, prolonged HOB elevation above 30°, donut devices, and powders or cornstarch. The highlighted practices need correction.
questions.takeaway: No rubbing, no donuts, no powder, and HOB ≤ 30° when possible.
questions.hintContent: Recall the list of prevention practices the text says to avoid, and the HOB limit for reducing shear.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a ‘needs further teaching’ item — you are highlighting the WRONG practices, not the correct ones.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Evaluation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is comparing this week's assessment of a client's Stage 3 sacral pressure injury with last week's documentation. Click to highlight the findings that indicate the wound is progressing toward healing.
questions.passage: Wound {{length decreased from 5.0 cm to 3.8 cm}}. {{Beefy red, granular tissue covers 90% of the wound bed}}, and there is {{new pink epithelial tissue along the wound margin}}. {{Moderate thick, green drainage with a foul odor after cleansing}}. {{Undermining now extends 2 cm (previously 1 cm)}}. {{Periwound skin is white and wrinkled}}. {{A new patch of black eschar is present at the wound base}}.
optionRationales: Healing. Decreasing dimensions measured the same way each week show the wound is filling and contracting.
Healing. Healthy granulation tissue is beefy red, moist, and granular.
Healing. Epithelial cells migrating from the margin are the final step in wound closure.
Not healing. Thick, green, foul-smelling drainage is purulent and suggests infection.
Not healing. Increasing undermining means tissue destruction beneath the edges.
Not healing. White, wrinkled periwound skin is maceration from excess moisture.
Not healing. New black eschar is necrotic tissue that must be debrided (RYB: black = debride).
questions.rationale: Signs of healing include decreasing size, healthy red granulation, and new epithelium at the edges. Purulent drainage, increasing undermining, maceration, and new necrotic tissue indicate infection or deterioration and require the care plan to be modified.
questions.takeaway: Healing = smaller, redder (granulation), and pink edges; not pus, maceration, or new eschar.
questions.hintContent: Recall what healthy granulation and epithelial tissue look like and what the RYB color system says about a red wound.
questions.hintStrategy: Mentally label each finding ‘better’ or ‘worse’ than last week; highlight only the ‘better’ ones.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Risk Factors (Excessive Body Heat)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client on bed rest with pneumonia has a temperature of 39.2 °C (102.6 °F). A nursing student asks why the fever increases the client's risk for pressure injury. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Fever raises the metabolic rate and oxygen demand, so tissue under pressure becomes ischemic faster.”
“Fever lowers capillary pressure to zero, so any contact with the bed stops blood flow.”
“Fever makes the skin thicker and less elastic, so it tears when the client is turned.”
“Fever causes the kidneys to lose protein, so the skin loses the padding over the bones.”
optionRationales: Correct. Excessive body heat increases the metabolic rate and oxygen demand, which worsens ischemia in tissue that is already under pressure.
Incorrect. Fever does not stop capillary flow; the problem is that tissues need more oxygen than a compressed capillary bed can deliver.
Incorrect. Fever does not thicken the skin; loss of elasticity is an age-related change.
Incorrect. Fever does not cause renal protein loss; loss of padding comes from inadequate nutrition.
questions.rationale: The slides list excessive body heat as a risk factor: fever increases metabolic rate and oxygen demand, so tissue compressed over a bony prominence becomes ischemic more quickly. Clients with fever need close skin assessment and consistent repositioning.
questions.takeaway: Fever = ↑ metabolic rate + ↑ O₂ demand = faster ischemia under pressure.
questions.hintContent: Recall what excessive body heat does to the tissue's need for oxygen.
questions.hintStrategy: Link the cue in the stem (fever) to a mechanism of ischemia; eliminate options that describe effects fever does not have.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Risk Factors for Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical-surgical unit is reviewing four assigned clients. Which client is at greatest risk for developing a pressure injury?
options: A 45-year-old with a casted wrist fracture who walks independently and eats 100% of every meal
A 29-year-old with a new T4 spinal cord injury, fever of 38.9 °C (102 °F), and bowel incontinence
A 70-year-old with heart failure who walks in the hall three times daily and is continent of urine
A 62-year-old with diabetes who sits in a chair most of the day and shifts position independently
optionRationales: Incorrect. Independent ambulation and adequate intake mean low risk despite the fracture.
Correct. Absent sensation and mobility below T4, excess body heat raising oxygen demand, and moisture from incontinence combine several major risk factors.
Incorrect. Age and heart failure raise risk slightly, but this client is mobile and continent.
Incorrect. Sitting increases ischial pressure, but the client can sense discomfort and shift weight independently.
questions.rationale: Risk is greatest when multiple factors combine: diminished sensation (cannot feel warning signs), immobility, excess body heat, and moisture. The client with an acute spinal cord injury has all of these; the others have one factor or none and can protect themselves.
questions.takeaway: Count risk factors: no sensation + no movement + heat + moisture = highest risk.
questions.hintContent: Recall the slide list of risk factors: immobility, nutrition, incontinence, mental status, sensation, body heat, age, and chronic disease.
questions.hintStrategy: Tally the risk factors for each client and weigh them: one factor offset by intact sensation and independent movement carries less risk than several factors acting together.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Pressure Injuries – Overview; Supportive Devices
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with obesity was found on the floor at home after lying on the right side for about 10 hours. The skin over the right hip is red and does not blanch. The nurse explains to the client's family how the injury developed. Complete the nurse's explanation.
questions.template: When external pressure is greater than capillary pressure of about {0}, blood flow decreases and the tissue becomes {1}. If pressure is not relieved, the tissue {2}.

options: 32 mm Hg
60 mm Hg
120 mm Hg
edematous from lymph overload
ischemic
hyperemic and stronger
undergoes necrosis and may break down into an ulcer
returns to normal as soon as the skin color improves
becomes stronger as collagen is deposited

questions.rationale: Supportive devices aim to keep external pressure below capillary pressure (about 32 mm Hg). Prolonged pressure above this level decreases blood flow, causing ischemia; unrelieved ischemia leads to tissue necrosis and an ulcer. Nonblanchable redness of intact skin is a Stage 1 injury that must be offloaded and reassessed.
questions.takeaway: Pressure > 32 mm Hg → ↓ flow → ischemia → necrosis → ulcer.
questions.hintContent: Recall the capillary pressure number used as the goal for support surfaces and the slide pathway from pressure to ulcer.
questions.hintStrategy: Each blank builds on the one before. Once you know blood flow drops, ask what that does to the tissue, and then what happens if it continues.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Risk Factors for Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing data for an 88-year-old resident of a long-term care facility who has advanced dementia. Which findings increase this resident's risk for pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Weight decreased from 54 kg (119 lb) to 49 kg (108 lb) over the past month
Needs moderate assistance to move in bed and slides down in the wheelchair
Incontinent of urine several times per shift
Walks to the dining room with a walker three times daily
Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL
Drinks about 1,800 mL of fluid daily
optionRationales: Correct. A 9% loss in 1 month signals malnutrition, loss of padding over bony prominences, and poor tissue repair.
Correct. Limited mobility and sliding produce sustained pressure plus friction and shear.
Correct. Urine moisture macerates skin and lowers its tolerance to pressure and friction.
Incorrect. Regular ambulation is protective.
Incorrect. This hemoglobin is within normal limits and supports oxygen delivery.
Incorrect. Adequate fluid intake supports skin turgor and perfusion.
questions.rationale: Risk factors include inadequate nutrition (weight loss), immobility, friction and shear, and moisture from incontinence, in addition to decreased mental status and advanced age. Ambulation, normal hemoglobin, and adequate hydration are protective.
questions.takeaway: Weight loss, immobility, shear, and moisture — watch for the combination in older adults.
questions.hintContent: Recall how nutrition, mobility, and moisture each affect tissue tolerance to pressure.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true/false: does this finding increase risk, or is it normal/protective?

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Risk Factors (Advanced Age)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The daughter of an 86-year-old client asks why her mother developed a pressure injury after only 2 days in bed. Which age-related change should the nurse include in the explanation?
options: “Older adults sweat much more, which keeps the skin constantly soaked.”
“Older skin has a thicker outer layer that traps heat against the tissue.”
“Older adults have higher capillary pressure, so the bed presses harder on the skin.”
“Older skin is thinner and less elastic, with less oil and poorer circulation.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sweat production decreases with age; older skin tends to be dry.
Incorrect. The skin of older adults becomes thinner, not thicker.
Incorrect. Aging does not raise capillary pressure; a higher capillary pressure would actually protect tissue.
Correct. Thinner, less elastic skin with decreased oil, decreased circulation, and increased dryness tolerates pressure poorly.
questions.rationale: Advanced age is a pressure injury risk factor because the skin becomes thinner and less elastic, with decreased oil, decreased circulation, and increased dryness. Older adults may also have chronic conditions (diabetes, cardiovascular disease) that further impair circulation and healing.
questions.takeaway: Aging skin: thin, less elastic, dry, and poorly perfused.
questions.hintContent: Recall the age-related skin changes listed on the risk-factor slide.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that describe changes opposite to what happens with aging skin.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention – Repositioning (Positions)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client on bed rest has a Stage 2 pressure injury on the sacrum and an area of nonblanchable erythema over the right greater trochanter. The nurse is about to turn the client off the back. Which position is most appropriate?
options: Left side-lying at 90° with the top leg resting directly on the bottom leg
Supine with the head of the bed at 45° and the knees gatched for comfort
Left 30° lateral tilt with pillows behind the back and between the knees
Right 30° lateral tilt so the client can face the door and reach the call light
optionRationales: Incorrect. A 90° side-lying position places full body weight on the left trochanter, and the legs touching creates pressure between bony knees and ankles.
Incorrect. This keeps the client on the injured sacrum and increases shear with HOB above 30°.
Correct. A 30° tilt to the left relieves the sacrum and the injured right trochanter without loading the left trochanter directly; pillows keep bony prominences apart.
Incorrect. Tilting to the right loads the right trochanter, which already has a Stage 1 injury.
questions.rationale: Avoid positioning a client on an existing pressure injury. The 30° lateral tilt distributes weight across the buttock rather than the trochanter or sacrum. Pillows between the knees and ankles prevent bone-on-bone contact.
questions.takeaway: Use a 30° tilt, and never position on an existing injury.
questions.hintContent: Recall which bony prominence bears weight in 90° side-lying compared with a 30° tilt.
questions.hintStrategy: First eliminate any option that places weight on either existing injury, then compare the remaining angles.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Implementation (Chair Positioning)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: An 80-year-old client with heart failure and limited mobility at a rehabilitation facility prefers to sit up in a chair for much of the day. The client can follow simple directions. Which interventions should the nurse include to protect the client's skin while sitting? Select all that apply.
options: Reposition the client at least every hour while in the chair
Use a seating cushion designed to redistribute pressure
Place a foam ring cushion under the buttocks
Support the feet on the floor or a footrest so the thighs are level
Recline the chair so the client slides forward off the sacrum
Cue the client to shift weight about every 15 minutes
optionRationales: Correct. Seated clients bear high ischial pressure and should be repositioned at least every hour.
Correct. Pressure-redistributing cushions reduce peak pressure on the ischial tuberosities.
Incorrect. Ring cushions reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue and are avoided.
Correct. Supported feet and level thighs spread weight across the thighs instead of the ischia and prevent sliding.
Incorrect. Sliding forward creates shear across the sacrum and coccyx.
Correct. Clients who are able should shift weight every 15–30 minutes (commonly taught as every 15 minutes).
questions.rationale: When sitting, pressure concentrates on the ischial tuberosities. Protective measures include limiting sitting time, hourly repositioning, frequent self-weight shifts, a pressure-redistributing cushion, and good posture with feet supported. Donut devices and sliding positions increase injury.
questions.takeaway: Chair: reposition hourly, shift weight often, proper cushion, feet supported — never a donut.
questions.hintContent: Recall how often seated clients should be repositioned compared with bedbound clients, and which devices the text says to avoid.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option independently. Watch for options that sound comfortable but create shear or reduce blood flow.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Implementation (Skin Integrity)
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is observing an LPN provide care to a client at high risk for pressure injury. Which action by the LPN requires the RN to intervene?
options: Raising the head of the bed to 30° after the client finishes lunch
Using a draw sheet with a UAP to move the client up in bed
Massaging lotion into a reddened area over the client's sacrum
Applying a dimethicone barrier cream after perineal care
optionRationales: Appropriate. Keeping the HOB at 30° or lower reduces shear.
Appropriate. Lifting with a draw sheet avoids friction and shear.
Requires intervention. Massage over bony prominences or reddened areas damages capillaries and deeper tissue and is avoided.
Appropriate. Barrier creams such as dimethicone protect skin from moisture.
questions.rationale: The implementation slide directs the nurse to avoid massage over bony prominences, manage moisture, and use proper turning and transferring techniques. Massaging a reddened sacrum can worsen deep tissue damage, so the RN intervenes.
questions.takeaway: Never massage a reddened bony prominence.
questions.hintContent: Recall which skin-care practice the implementation slide specifically says to avoid.
questions.hintStrategy: This item asks for the unsafe action. Check each option against the slide list of skin integrity interventions.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention – Nutrition
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 74-year-old client has a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury and eats about 50% of meals. Kidney function is normal. For each potential intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Monitor weight, albumin, hemoglobin, and lymphocyte count
Offer high-calorie, high-protein oral supplements between meals
Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL/day to reduce wound drainage
Encourage foods rich in vitamins A and C, zinc, and iron
Limit protein to prevent weight gain while the client is on bed rest
optionRationales: Indicated. These are the values the slides list for monitoring nutritional status.
Indicated. Supplements are used when a client is nutritionally compromised.
Not indicated. Adequate hydration supports circulation and tissue repair; fluid restriction is not a wound treatment.
Indicated. Vitamins A and C, zinc, and iron are key nutrients for skin integrity and healing.
Not indicated. Protein is essential for tissue repair; restricting it delays healing.
questions.rationale: Adequate intake means fewer pressure injuries and better healing. Key nutrients are protein, calories, vitamins A and C, zinc, and iron. The nurse monitors weight, lymphocyte count, albumin, and hemoglobin, uses supplements when the client is nutritionally compromised, and consults the dietitian.
questions.takeaway: Feed the wound: protein, calories, vitamins A and C, zinc, iron — and trend weight and labs.
questions.hintContent: Recall the key nutrients and the monitoring values on the nutrition-prevention slide.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each row on its own: does it supply or monitor what the healing wound needs, or does it take something away?

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention – Skin Hygiene
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is supervising a UAP who is providing morning care to a client with a Braden score of 12 on a low-air-loss mattress. Which actions by the UAP require the RN to intervene? Select all that apply.
options: Bathing the client with hot water to stimulate circulation
Placing three folded incontinence pads under the client on the mattress
Using a lift sheet with a coworker to reposition the client
Applying a dimethicone barrier cream after perineal care
Dusting cornstarch into the skin folds under the abdomen
Reporting a red area that has not faded 30 minutes after turning
optionRationales: Intervene. Hot water dries and damages the skin; use warm water and mild cleansers.
Intervene. Multiple linen layers block the airflow and pressure redistribution of a low-air-loss surface.
Appropriate. A lift sheet with two people prevents friction and shear.
Appropriate. Dimethicone barrier products protect skin from moisture.
Intervene. Powders and cornstarch clump with moisture and irritate the skin.
Appropriate. Persistent redness should be reported so the RN can assess it.
questions.rationale: UAPs can perform hygiene and repositioning, but the RN must correct unsafe practices: hot water, layering linens on specialty surfaces, and powders. Gentle cleansing, barrier creams, lift sheets, and prompt reporting are correct.
questions.takeaway: One layer on a specialty bed; warm (not hot) water; barrier cream, not powder.
questions.hintContent: Recall the slide list of what to use and avoid for skin hygiene, and how specialty mattresses work.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a ‘requires intervention’ item — you are selecting the UNSAFE actions.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Implementation (Teaching)
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with a T8 spinal cord injury who uses a manual wheelchair is being discharged home. The nurse evaluates the client's understanding of pressure-injury prevention. For each client statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or indicates a need for further teaching.
rows: “I'll use a long-handled mirror every day to check my buttocks and heels.”
“I'll do a lean or push-up to shift my weight about every 15 minutes in my chair.”
“Since I can't feel my buttocks, I'll shift my weight when I start to feel uncomfortable.”
“If a red spot doesn't fade 30 minutes after I'm off it, I'll stay off it and call the clinic.”
“I'll cut back on protein so I don't gain weight from sitting all day.”
optionRationales: Shows understanding. Daily self-inspection with a mirror detects early injury in areas the client cannot see or feel.
Shows understanding. Frequent weight shifts relieve ischial pressure.
Needs teaching. The client lacks sensation below T8 and cannot rely on discomfort; shifts must be done on a schedule.
Shows understanding. Persistent redness means injury; the area must be offloaded and evaluated.
Needs teaching. Adequate protein is essential for skin integrity; weight is managed through overall calories and activity.
questions.rationale: Clients with spinal cord injury have lost the protective warning of pain. Teaching emphasizes scheduled weight shifts, daily skin inspection, prompt action on persistent redness, and adequate protein.
questions.takeaway: No sensation = scheduled pressure relief, not ‘when it hurts.’
questions.hintContent: Recall why diminished sensation is a key risk factor and what adequate nutrition contributes to skin integrity.
questions.hintStrategy: Read each statement for a hidden flaw — one depends on a sense the client no longer has.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention – Repositioning (Positions)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client on bed rest has been lying supine for most of the shift. Which bony prominences should the nurse inspect most closely for pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Occiput
Sacrum and coccyx
Heels
Anterior knees
Forehead and chin
Scapulae
optionRationales: Correct. The back of the head bears weight in the supine position.
Correct. The sacrum and coccyx are the most common pressure sites when supine.
Correct. The heels rest directly on the mattress when supine unless they are floated.
Incorrect. The anterior knees bear weight in the prone position.
Incorrect. The forehead and chin bear weight in the prone position.
Correct. The shoulder blades bear weight in the supine position.
questions.rationale: Pressure injuries form over the bony prominences that bear weight in each position. In the supine position, these are the occiput, scapulae, elbows, sacrum and coccyx, and heels. The anterior knees, iliac crests, and face are pressure points in the prone position.
questions.takeaway: Supine: occiput, scapulae, elbows, sacrum/coccyx, heels.
questions.hintContent: Picture the client lying on the back and identify which bony areas touch the mattress.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate every site that bears weight only when the client is lying face-down.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Implementation (Moisture Management)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse is providing care after a client at high risk for pressure injury is incontinent of liquid stool. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Perform hand hygiene, apply clean gloves, and remove the soiled pad
Cleanse the perineal skin gently with a mild cleanser and warm water
Pat the skin dry without rubbing
Apply a thin layer of barrier cream such as dimethicone
Place a single breathable underpad and reposition the client off the sacrum
questions.rationale: Remove the irritant promptly, cleanse gently with a mild agent and warm (not hot) water, pat dry to avoid friction, and protect the skin with a barrier before placing a single breathable pad and repositioning. This protects skin from moisture and enzymes that cause maceration.
questions.takeaway: Remove → cleanse → pat dry → protect → reposition.
questions.hintContent: Recall why friction and moisture both damage skin and where a barrier product fits in skin care.
questions.hintStrategy: A barrier can only work on clean, dry skin — work backward from that.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: During a dressing change, the nurse assesses a client's coccyx wound that measures 3 × 2 × 0.5 cm. The wound bed has red granulation tissue and visible yellow fat, with yellow slough covering about 20% of the base. No muscle, tendon, or bone is visible or palpable. How should the nurse document this wound?
options: Stage 2 pressure injury
Stage 3 pressure injury
Stage 4 pressure injury
Stage 1 pressure injury
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stage 2 is partial thickness; fat is not visible.
Correct. Full-thickness loss into subcutaneous tissue (visible fat) without muscle, tendon, or bone is Stage 3.
Incorrect. Stage 4 requires damage to muscle, bone, or supporting structures.
Incorrect. Stage 1 is intact skin with nonblanchable redness; this wound is open and full thickness.
questions.rationale: Visible fat means full-thickness loss into subcutaneous tissue; the absence of muscle, tendon, or bone keeps it at Stage 3.
questions.takeaway: See fat = at least Stage 3; see bone, tendon, or muscle = Stage 4.
questions.hintContent: Recall the deepest tissue layer involved in each of the four stages.
questions.hintStrategy: Find the deepest structure described, then check whether slough hides enough of the base to prevent staging.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Diagnosis
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 75-year-old client on bed rest has a Braden score of 12. The skin is intact, and all reddened areas blanch and fade after turning. Which nursing diagnosis best describes the client's skin?
options: Potential for impaired skin integrity
Risk for infection related to an open wound
Impaired skin integrity
Situational low self-esteem
optionRationales: Correct. A high-risk Braden score with intact skin fits a potential (risk) diagnosis.
Incorrect. There is no open wound.
Incorrect. The skin is intact; there is no actual impairment yet.
Incorrect. Nothing in the data suggests a problem with self-esteem.
questions.rationale: Possible nursing diagnoses for pressure injuries include potential for impaired skin integrity, impaired skin integrity, risk for infection, underweight, compromised dignity, and situational low self-esteem. A client with high risk but intact skin has a potential problem; "impaired skin integrity" is used once the skin is broken or a Stage 1 injury is present.
questions.takeaway: Intact skin + high risk = potential for impaired skin integrity.
questions.hintContent: Recall the difference between an actual nursing diagnosis and a potential (risk) diagnosis.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask whether the problem already exists or could develop; choose the diagnosis that matches the data.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries (Stage II)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing skin findings recorded for several clients. For each finding, indicate whether it should be classified as a Stage 2 pressure injury.
rows: Shallow open wound with a pink, moist bed over the ischial tuberosity of a client who sits all day
Intact blister filled with clear fluid on the heel of a client on bed rest
Intact skin over the sacrum with redness that does not blanch
Full-thickness wound over the hip with visible yellow fat
Ruptured blister over the elbow with a moist, pink base
optionRationales: Stage 2. Partial-thickness loss with a shallow, pink, moist bed.
Stage 2. A clear-fluid blister is partial-thickness loss of the epidermis.
Not Stage 2. Intact skin with nonblanchable redness is Stage 1.
Not Stage 2. Visible fat means full-thickness loss — Stage 3.
Stage 2. A ruptured blister with a pink, moist base is partial-thickness loss.
questions.rationale: Stage 2 is partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and possibly the dermis: a shallow, open, pink wound or an intact or ruptured clear blister. Intact skin with nonblanchable redness is Stage 1, and visible fat means full-thickness loss (Stage 3).
questions.takeaway: Stage 2 = shallow and partial thickness: pink open area or blister.
questions.hintContent: Recall the depth of tissue loss that defines Stage 2 and how it differs from Stages 1 and 3.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask for each row: is the skin intact, partially lost, or lost through its full thickness?

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention – Supportive Devices
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing pressure-redistribution devices with a newly hired UAP who will care for a client at high risk for pressure injury. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: Support surfaces aim to keep pressure on the skin below capillary pressure of about {0}. The client's heels are protected with {1}. The UAP should never use {2} because they reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue.

options: 32 mm Hg
80 mm Hg
120 mm Hg
tight elastic wraps around the ankles
heel protectors or pillows that lift the heels off the bed
a rolled towel placed directly under each heel
foam overlays
pillows and wedges
doughnut (ring) cushions

questions.rationale: The goal of supportive devices is to keep external pressure below capillary pressure (32 mm Hg). Overlays, specialty beds, pillows, wedges, and heel protectors offload pressure points and reduce pressure injuries by about 60%. Doughnut devices reduce blood flow and cause injury, so they are avoided.
questions.takeaway: Keep pressure < 32 mm Hg; float heels; no doughnuts.
questions.hintContent: Recall the capillary pressure goal and the device the slides say to avoid.
questions.hintStrategy: Answer each blank separately. For the heels, choose the option that removes pressure rather than moving it to a smaller area.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Four Stages of Pressure Injuries (Stage IV)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is measuring and assessing a client's sacral pressure injury after cleansing. Which findings, if present, would indicate that the wound is a Stage 4 pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Bone palpable at the base with a sterile applicator
Visible tendon in the wound bed
Visible subcutaneous fat with no deeper structures
Exposed muscle at the base
Undermining of 1 cm beneath the lower wound edge
Red, moist granulation tissue along the wound walls
optionRationales: Correct. Palpable or exposed bone is Stage 4.
Correct. Exposed tendon, a supporting structure, is Stage 4.
Incorrect. Visible fat without deeper structures is Stage 3.
Correct. Exposed muscle is Stage 4.
Incorrect. Undermining can occur in deep wounds of either Stage 3 or Stage 4; it does not define the stage.
Incorrect. Granulation tissue shows healing activity, not the depth of the original injury.
questions.rationale: Stage 4 is full-thickness skin loss with tissue necrosis or damage to muscle, bone, or supporting structures such as tendon. Undermining and granulation tissue are wound features, not staging criteria.
questions.takeaway: Stage 4 = you can see or feel the ‘supporting structures’ (muscle, tendon, bone).
questions.hintContent: Recall which tissue structures define Stage 4 compared with Stage 3.
questions.hintStrategy: Each option is independent — ask whether that single finding alone would place the wound in Stage 4.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Evaluation (Prioritization)
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse receives hand-off report for four clients on a medical unit. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a Stage 2 sacral pressure injury whose dressing edge is rolled
A client with a Braden score of 12 who was last repositioned 2½ hours ago and reports sacral soreness
A client with a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury who is scheduled for a dressing change this morning
A client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury who is newly confused, with HR 116 and BP 88/50
optionRationales: Not first. A rolled edge needs attention soon but is not life-threatening.
Not first. This client needs repositioning promptly (which can be delegated), but the condition is not an immediate threat to life.
Not first. A routine scheduled dressing change is stable care.
First. New confusion, tachycardia, and hypotension in a client with a deep wound suggest a spreading, systemic infection — a life-threatening complication.
questions.rationale: Deep pressure injuries can become infected, and systemic signs (altered mental status, tachycardia, hypotension) take priority over local wound issues and routine prevention. The overdue repositioning can be delegated to a UAP while the nurse assesses the unstable client.
questions.takeaway: Systemic instability beats local wound problems.
questions.hintContent: Recall the signs that a wound infection is affecting the whole body.
questions.hintStrategy: Use unstable vs. stable: which client has abnormal vital signs or a change in mental status?

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Implementation (Delegation)
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is making assignments with an LPN on a medical-surgical unit. Which task related to pressure-injury care is most appropriate to assign to the LPN?
options: Performing the prescribed dressing change on a Stage 3 wound staged by the RN today
Completing the initial admission skin assessment and staging for a newly admitted client
Developing the pressure-injury prevention teaching plan for a client going home today
Determining the stage of a new open area found on a client's heel
optionRationales: Correct. Performing an established, prescribed dressing change on a stable client is within LPN scope; the LPN reports changes to the RN.
Incorrect. The initial admission assessment and staging are RN responsibilities.
Incorrect. Developing a teaching plan requires RN-level planning; the LPN may reinforce teaching.
Incorrect. Interpreting and staging a new finding is an RN assessment.
questions.rationale: RNs retain initial assessment, staging of new findings, care planning, teaching plans, and evaluation. LPNs can perform established procedures (such as ordered dressing changes) for stable clients, collect data, and reinforce teaching.
questions.takeaway: LPN: established procedures on stable clients. RN: assess, stage new findings, plan, teach, evaluate.
questions.hintContent: Recall the scope of practice differences between RN and LPN for assessment, planning, and procedures.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether the client situation is new or already established and stable, and whether the task requires interpreting data or creating a plan.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Planning
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse is writing expected outcomes for a client with a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury. Which outcome statements are correctly written? Select all that apply.
options: The client will state three ways to protect the skin before discharge.
The sacral wound will decrease in length and width by 25% within 2 weeks.
The nurse will turn the client every 2 hours.
The client will understand the importance of good nutrition.
The client will have no new areas of nonblanchable erythema during hospitalization.
The client’s wound will heal quickly.
optionRationales: Correct. Client-centered, measurable (three ways), and time-bound (before discharge).
Correct. Measurable (25%) and time-bound (2 weeks).
Incorrect. This is a nursing intervention written about the nurse, not a client outcome.
Incorrect. ‘Understand’ is not observable or measurable.
Correct. Measurable and time-bound; it reflects prevention of further breakdown.
Incorrect. ‘Quickly’ is vague and has no measurable criterion or time frame.
questions.rationale: Expected outcomes are client-centered, specific, measurable, realistic, and time-limited. Interventions describe what the nurse does, and verbs like ‘understand’ or vague words like ‘quickly’ cannot be evaluated.
questions.takeaway: Outcomes: the client will [measurable verb] [criterion] by [time].
questions.hintContent: Recall the parts of a well-written outcome: subject, measurable verb, criterion, and time frame.
questions.hintStrategy: For each statement, ask ‘Who is the subject?’ and ‘How would I measure this?’

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Diagnosis (Compromised Dignity)
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 67-year-old client with a Stage 4 sacral pressure injury tells the nurse, “I can smell my own wound. I don't want my grandchildren to visit anymore.” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “The odor comes from bacteria, so it's safer if the children don't visit for now.”
“Try not to worry. Most visitors don't notice the smell at all.”
“You sound embarrassed. Let's plan ways to control the odor before they visit.”
“I'll spray some air freshener around the room before your visitors arrive.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This reinforces isolation and is not accurate; standard precautions and a covered wound protect visitors.
Incorrect. False reassurance dismisses the client’s feelings and closes communication.
Correct. Reflecting the feeling acknowledges compromised dignity, and planning odor control (timely cleansing and dressing changes) addresses the cause.
Incorrect. Masking odor does not address the client’s feelings or the source of odor, and sprays can irritate.
questions.rationale: Pressure injuries can cause compromised dignity and situational low self-esteem. Therapeutic communication acknowledges the feeling and involves the client in solutions such as timely wound cleansing and dressing changes.
questions.takeaway: Acknowledge the feeling, then solve the problem together.
questions.hintContent: Recall the psychosocial nursing diagnoses associated with pressure injuries and the features of therapeutic responses.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate responses that give false reassurance, change the subject, or promote isolation.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Nursing Process – Evaluation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation

tabs.title: Care Plan
tabs.html:

  • Cleanse with normal saline and apply a moist dressing daily
  • Oral nutrition supplement twice daily

questions.stem: Refer to the Wound Measurements and Care Plan for a client with a Stage 3 sacral pressure injury. Complete the nurse's evaluation.
questions.template: The wound is {0}. Because there has been no progress toward healing in {1}, the nurse should {2}.

options: showing expected progress
deteriorating
healing by primary intention
2 weeks
24 hours
6 months
continue the current plan unchanged for another month
reassess the client and wound and collaborate to revise the plan
switch to a donut cushion to fully offload the sacrum

questions.rationale: The wound is getting larger and deeper, with increasing slough and drainage — it is deteriorating. When goals are not met, the nurse reassesses and modifies the care plan; a pressure injury that shows no progress over about 2 weeks calls for this. Pressure injuries heal by secondary intention, and doughnut cushions are harmful.
questions.takeaway: No progress in 2 weeks → reassess and revise; don’t keep doing what isn’t working.
questions.hintContent: Recall what healing looks like in serial measurements and the time frame after which a non-healing wound triggers reassessment.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare week 1 with week 3 for each column; the direction of change answers the first blank.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · Prevention – Supportive Devices
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews new prescriptions for a client with a Stage 2 sacral pressure injury. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider before implementing it?
options: Reposition at least every 2 hours using pillows and wedges
Dietitian consult for protein and calorie supplements
Apply heel protectors while the client is in bed
Place a doughnut cushion under the sacrum when the client sits up
optionRationales: Appropriate. Repositioning at least every 2 hours with positioning devices is a standard outcome and intervention.
Appropriate. Supplements and dietitian input support healing when intake is poor.
Appropriate. Heel protectors offload the heels.
Clarify. Doughnut devices reduce blood flow to the surrounding tissue and cause injury; a pressure-redistributing seat cushion is used instead.
questions.rationale: Supportive devices are chosen to keep external pressure below capillary pressure (about 32 mm Hg). Pillows, wedges, heel protectors, overlays, and specialty beds are appropriate. Doughnut devices concentrate pressure on the ring and reduce blood flow, so the nurse questions that prescription.
questions.takeaway: Question any order for a doughnut cushion.
questions.hintContent: Recall which supportive device the slides specifically say to avoid.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each prescription against the prevention slides; find the one that could harm the client.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · RYB Color Guide – Biosurgery (Maggots)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client has a nonhealing Stage 4 pressure injury on the right heel with necrotic tissue and adequate arterial blood flow. The provider recommends biosurgery with sterile maggots. After teaching, which statement by the client indicates understanding?
options: “The maggots will eat into healthy tissue too, so I'll need a skin graft after.”
“The larvae digest dead tissue and do little harm to healthy tissue.”
“The maggots stay in place permanently until my wound has fully closed.”
“This treatment means I no longer have to keep pressure off my heel.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Medical larvae digest necrotic tissue and cause minimal damage to healthy tissue.
Correct. Biosurgery uses sterile larvae to selectively digest necrotic tissue.
Incorrect. Larvae are applied in contained dressings for short cycles (commonly 2–4 days) and then removed; they are not permanent.
Incorrect. Offloading remains essential; debridement does not remove the cause of the injury.
questions.rationale: Biosurgery (maggot debridement therapy) places sterile larvae on nonhealing necrotic wounds; they digest dead tissue with minimal damage to healthy tissue and may be preferable to surgical debridement for some clients. Pressure relief and other wound care continue.
questions.takeaway: Maggots are selective debriders — they eat dead tissue, not healthy tissue.
questions.hintContent: Recall how biosurgery differs from sharp debridement in its effect on healthy tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: Teaching-evaluation items: pick the statement that is accurate, and watch for statements that drop other essential care.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Exemplar 21.B Pressure Injuries · RYB Color Guide – Debridement Methods

questions.stem: A nursing student is reviewing the debridement methods for a client whose pressure injury contains black necrotic tissue. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: A wet-to-dry dressing is an example of {0} debridement. Applying prescribed enzymes to the necrotic tissue is {1} debridement. A special dressing that captures drainage so the body's own enzymes break down dead tissue is {2} debridement. Removal of eschar with a scalpel by a surgeon is {3} debridement.

options: chemical
mechanical
sharp
autolytic
sharp
chemical
autolytic
mechanical
chemical
mechanical
sharp
autolytic

questions.rationale: The slides list debridement as sharp (surgeon with a scalpel), mechanical (wet-to-dry dressing), chemical (enzymes), autolytic (special dressings that capture drainage), and biosurgery (sterile maggots). Nurses can debride within limits; sharp debridement is performed by the surgeon.
questions.takeaway: Wet-to-dry = mechanical; enzymes = chemical; special dressings = autolytic; scalpel = sharp.
questions.hintContent: Recall the four named methods of debridement on the RYB slide and what each uses.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the tool in each sentence (dressing, enzyme, special dressing, scalpel) to its method.
